messages.author: 1004dd6f66bb10c3
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Fwd: [stan-users] beta distribution
parts:
One problem is that we translate from unconstrained to constrained to
evaluate the log-density. This shows up with the gamma(0.01, 1) too,
whose left tail looks almost identical to the beta(0.01, 1)
distribution. If we have
x ~ gamma(0.01, 1)
then a typical draw for x is in the range of exp(-1000) to 5 or so.
But of course exp(-1000)=0 at double precision, and log(0) is outside
of the support of the unconstrained variable.

A workaround is to do something like this for the gamma(a, b):

parameters {
real logx;
}
transformed parameters {
real x;
x <- exp(logx);
}
model {
lp__ <- lp__ + a * logx - b * x;
}

or this for the beta(a, b):

parameters {
real logitx;
}
transformed parameters {
real x;
x <- inv_logit(logitx);
}
model {
lp__ <- lp__ - a * log(1 + exp(-logitx)) - b * log(1 + exp(logitx));
}

But that's not ideal. I'm not sure what we can do about this within
our current architecture, which really wants to transform beta r.v.s
to [0, 1] and gamma r.v.s to [0, inf].

Matt

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Fwd: [stan-users] beta distribution

On Monday, February 25, 2013 4:57:42 PM UTC-5, Matt Hoffman wrote:
But that's not ideal. I'm not sure what we can do about this within
our current architecture, which really wants to transform beta r.v.s
to [0, 1] and gamma r.v.s to [0, inf].

All true, but in this particular case, the RV was data and not being transformed. So, it seems that for alpha very small and beta very large and x close to zero, the gradient of the log density blows up. Possibly the beta distribution is inappropriate for these data but it would be nice if we could come up with a solution to our numerical problems.

Ben

messages.author: 1004dd6f66bb10c3
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Fwd: [stan-users] beta distribution
parts:
Ah. Might the problem be that there's a 0 in the data? That 0 means you compute
–(a – 1) * ∞
which is big trouble for any value of a that's not 1. On the
unconstrained scale, there's actually no valid setting of a. But even
on the constrained scale, the prior assigns zero probability to a=1,
so you're guaranteed that the log-density of the data will be either
infinity or negative infinity. What happens if you replace the 0 with
0.001?

Matt

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: logit_beta
parts:
We could pretty easily add a version of beta for logit-scaled parameters
directly,

logit_beta(y|a,b) = beta(inv_logit(y)|a,b) * |d/du inv_logit(u)|_y,

which is arithmetically stable for y after a bit of algebra,

log logit_beta(y|a,b) = alpha * log_sum_exp(0,y)
+ beta * log_sum_exp(0,-y)
+ lgamma(a + b) - lgamma(a) - lgamma(b).

But what should we do if a or b is close to 0?

We have a further issue when a and b in beta(a,b) are themselves
parameters, becuase what's really going on is beta(exp(a'),exp(b'))
where a' and b' the unconstrained parameters being sampled by HMC/NUTS.

If inv_logit(y) is used as a probability parameter in
bernoulli or binomial, we can deal with it directly using bernoulli_logit
and binomial_logit. So an explicit beta binomial model would be

logit_theta ~ logit_beta(a,b);
n ~ binomial_logit(N,logit_theta);

where inv_logit(logit_theta) has the same distribution as theta under
the standard parameterization,

theta ~ beta(a,b);
n ~ binomial(N,y);

The logit version should be more efficient and more arithmetically
stable because we don't have to do any transforms of the parameters.

- Bob
